clue.text: Dance-music from South America by Academy orchestra

parts.note: RA stands for the Royal Academy (of Arts)
a band is a group of musicians playing together, a small orchestra

explanation.surface: A piece of Latin American dance music played by a college orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' simply places the pieces side by side. The Royal Academy, RA, is the London art institution.
explanation.definitionFit: A sarabande is a slow stately Spanish dance in triple time, and also the music written for it.

clue.text: Area where dry rot has turned up

parts.note: sec is French for dry, used of wine

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the word rot is read upwards, from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A region of the house where dry rot has appeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has turned up' reads like 'appeared', but turns ROT into TOR. 'where' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A sector is a distinct zone or part of a larger region or field.

clue.text: Respectable theatre with high-grade company

parts.note: rep is short for repertory theatre
U stands for upper-class, the top grade socially
a table is the company seated around one, as in the whole table laughed

explanation.surface: A theatre that is well regarded, with a first-rate troupe of actors.
explanation.walkthrough: U-and-non-U was a well-known British classification of upper-class versus other speech and habits.
explanation.definitionFit: A reputable person or firm is held in good regard, which is to be considered decent and honourable.

clue.text: Millais' publicity work for cake firm

definitions.text: Millais' publicity work for cake firm

parts.words: Millais' publicity work for cake firm
parts.note: the painter's portrait of a curly-haired boy was bought by Pears and used in its soap advertisements, the firm making cakes of soap

explanation.surface: A Victorian painter's picture used to advertise a bakery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cake' suggests a bakery, but the firm sold cakes of soap. The boy in the painting watches soap froth floating in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Everett Millais's 1886 painting of his grandson became the most famous Pears soap advertisement.

clue.text: Sounds like Miss Wallace taking Highway 50 in New York

indicators.note: the abbreviation for New York takes the other pieces inside it, holding them

parts.note: the El is New York's elevated railway, a raised way above the streets
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: An American performer named Wallace driving along a highway in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: Nellie Wallace was a British music-hall comedienne; the answer is a different spelling of her first name that is pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is pronounced identically to the music-hall star's first name, Nellie, though spelt differently.

clue.text: Rubber beetle?

explanation.surface: A question about some sort of rubber beetle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber' is not the material: it is one who rubs, and rubbing that causes soreness is chafing.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who chafes rubs abrasively; separately, the cockchafer and its relatives are large scarab beetles called chafers.

clue.text: Dress in order at home, naturally

parts.note: a habit is the dress worn by members of a religious order
taken as written

explanation.surface: Put on your clothes neatly when you are at home, of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in order' sounds like 'tidily', but refers to a religious order. 'naturally' qualifies 'home': the place where a creature lives in nature.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitat is the natural environment where an animal or plant normally lives.

clue.text: Severe expression father has now modified

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title

indicators.note: modified means changed, so the letters of now are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A stern look on Dad's face that has now altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modified' rearranges NOW as OWN. 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Knitting the brows to show disapproval gives a stern, disapproving look on the face.

clue.text: Disparages society leader in poor health

indicators.note: in places that letter inside the phrase for poor health

parts.note: to be run-down is to be tired and in poor health

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here the first letter of society

explanation.surface: A socialite who is unwell makes snide remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'society leader' gives just the first letter of society; 'in' then places it inside the phrase for being unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: To criticise someone unfairly or belittle them is to speak of them dismissively.

clue.text: Local correspondent at Gravesend put shirt on crooked horse

parts.note: the end of the word graves is its last letter, S
a T-shirt gives T for shirt
a ringer is a horse fraudulently substituted for another in a race

explanation.surface: A reporter in a Kent town bets everything on a fixed racehorse.
explanation.walkthrough: Gravesend is a town in Kent, but split as 'graves end' it gives S. To put your shirt on a horse is to bet everything on it, but here 'shirt' gives T and 'put on' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A stringer is a freelance journalist paid to report regularly on a particular area for a paper.

clue.text: Potential the railways have for a land developer

parts.note: potential is a capacity to develop, a synonym for capability
BR stood for British Rail, the old national railway network
to have something is to own it

explanation.surface: Wondering what potential the railways hold for a property developer.
explanation.walkthrough: BR, British Rail, was the UK's nationalised railway until the 1990s. Lancelot 'Capability' Brown earned his nickname by telling clients their estates had capability for improvement.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighteenth-century English landscape gardener reshaped the grounds of great country estates, so he literally developed land.

clue.text: Beat open-air theatre production

parts.note: out, as in out of doors, means in the open air
a play is a production staged in a theatre

explanation.surface: Praise for an outdoor theatre's staging of a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' looks like a description of the production's rhythm but is the verb meaning defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: To outplay an opponent is to play better than them and so defeat them.

clue.text: Sounded utterly monotonous!

parts.note: the clue plays on speaking in a single unvarying pitch: the word splits as being in one tone, utterly monotonous, while also meaning chanted or recited

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone's voice was dreary and flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounded' here means uttered, and the answer can be read as IN TONED, which is what a monotonous delivery is.
explanation.definitionFit: To intone is to recite or chant on a single sustained pitch, which is exactly a monotonous utterance.

clue.text: An attempt to get another gin is shame-making

parts.note: taken as written
to have a bash at something is to make an attempt

indicators.note: another version of the word gin, so its letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Asking for yet another gin after a failed attempt is embarrassing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' turns gin into ING. 'to get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Abashing someone makes them embarrassed and ashamed, so it is a shaming, discomfiting act.

clue.text: Breaks provisional direction explicitly including island

indicators.note: including means the phrase for explicitly holds the island's letter inside it

parts.note: to say something in terms, in so many words, is to say it explicitly

explanation.surface: A temporary instruction that expressly covers an island.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside IN TERMS, between its R and M.
explanation.definitionFit: An interim is an intervening period, an interval or pause between other events.

clue.text: Get the chuck shortly by starting wrongly

indicators.note: said shortly, the word is clipped, as in the casual spelling thro

parts.note: by in the sense of via, through, as in going by London

indicators.note: starting picks out the first letter of wrongly

explanation.surface: Someone is sacked soon after making a bad start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' trims THROUGH to the informal THRO; W comes from the start of 'wrongly'. 'Get the chuck' tempts as a phrase meaning be dismissed, but only 'chuck' defines, as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A chuck is an informal word for a toss, the act of hurling something.

clue.text: In old battlefield mire is all churned up

indicators.note: churned up mud is thoroughly disturbed, so the letters of the phrase are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: In a historic battlefield, all the mud is stirred up.
explanation.walkthrough: Ramillies, in present-day Belgium, was the site of Marlborough's victory over the French in 1706.
explanation.definitionFit: The village in Brabant gave its name to a major battle of the War of the Spanish Succession.

clue.text: Lofty approach about fruit being stolen

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
hips are the red fruit of the wild rose
hot is slang for stolen goods

explanation.surface: A high-handed approach to fruit that has been nicked.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf, the answer is a short lofted stroke onto the green, so 'Lofty' means high in the air, not haughty.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf a short shot played in the air to the green is a way of approaching the pin.

clue.text: Youth-leader in Orpington, perhaps — a laughable creature

indicators.note: in places the youth's leading letter inside the bird

parts.note: the Orpington is a breed of domestic chicken, so it is a hen
the leader of the word youth is its opening letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A youth club leader in a London suburb turns out to be a figure of fun.
explanation.walkthrough: Orpington is a town in south-east London, but here it is the chicken breed named after it. 'laughable' points to the animal's famous laugh-like call.
explanation.definitionFit: The spotted species of this African scavenger is known for a cackling call that sounds like laughter.

clue.text: A march I transposed in Ethiopian idiom

indicators.note: transposed means moved into another order, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: A piece of military music shifted into an Ethiopian key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transposed' and 'march' suggest music, but signal a rearrangement of A MARCH I.
explanation.definitionFit: Amharic is the main official language of Ethiopia, so it is an Ethiopian tongue or idiom.

clue.text: In time poor Rose becomes boring

indicators.note: in places the rearranged flower inside the word for time

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: poor suggests a bad state, so the letters of Rose are put into a different order

explanation.surface: Over time, a neglected rose becomes dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' anagrams the flower's letters and 'In' places them inside the word time, splitting it after its second letter; 'time' is fodder, not an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tiresome wears you out with monotony, so it is tedious and dull.

clue.text: Cook's vessel has no sails

explanation.surface: A chef's pot that lacks sails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' points to a ship, but the first sense is a kitchen pan used for steaming food.
explanation.definitionFit: A cook uses a steaming pan for vegetables; a steamship is driven by steam engines rather than wind on canvas.

clue.text: Clears, I hear, the stoppage

indicators.note: I hear signals that the word is what is heard, a word sounding the same

parts.note: to clear someone of blame is to free them

explanation.surface: Someone thinks a blockage has been removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A wage or price freeze is a halt, a stoppage of any change or movement.

clue.text: Unpopular doubles partner from Lincolnshire?

explanation.surface: Asking whether a disliked tennis doubles partner comes from Lincolnshire.
explanation.walkthrough: In tennis doubles, a player who cuts across to take shots meant for their partner is said to poach. 'The Lincolnshire Poacher' is the county's traditional folk song.
explanation.definitionFit: A partner who intercepts balls meant for you steals your shots; the Lincolnshire folk song names an illegal game-hunter.

clue.text: Psychiatrist a New-Dealer? That's pointless

indicators.note: new signals a new form, so the remaining letters of the word dealer are rearranged
the compass point east is taken out, so dealer loses that letter

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a Roosevelt-era reformer was useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New-Dealer' looks like a supporter of Roosevelt's New Deal, but 'New' is the anagram signal. 'pointless' removes an E (east) from DEALER, leaving DALER; 'New' rearranges it. Alfred Adler founded individual psychology.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Adler, an Austrian who broke from Freud, founded the school of individual psychology.

clue.text: Mrs Pat has right to be classified as a star

parts.note: Mrs Patrick Campbell, the Edwardian actress, was born Beatrice Stella Tanner and known as Stella

explanation.surface: An actress claiming the right to be billed as a star.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Patrick Campbell, nicknamed Mrs Pat, was a famous English stage actress for whom Shaw wrote Eliza Doolittle.
explanation.definitionFit: Stellar is the adjective for things relating to or belonging among the stars.

clue.text: On rising, old queen has herbal infusion

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the pieces are read upwards, so they appear backwards

parts.note: Anne was Queen of Great Britain from 1702 to 1714
has is shortened to 's

explanation.surface: When she gets up, a former queen takes a herbal tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' gives the 's of ANNE'S, which is read upwards as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Senna is a plant whose dried leaves and pods are steeped to make a laxative drink.

clue.text: Early example of Western imperialism …

parts.note: a medieval European realm that claimed descent from ancient Rome's imperial authority and was blessed by the Pope

explanation.surface: Pointing to the first instance of European empire-building, to be continued in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into 27 across, whose clue refers back to this answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The realm founded under Charlemagne and Otto I was a Western European imperial state lasting from the early Middle Ages until 1806.

clue.text: … this many times denied by Voltaire

definitions.text: this many times denied by Voltaire

parts.words: this many times denied by Voltaire
parts.note: Voltaire quipped that the empire of the previous clue was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire, so its name is denied on three counts

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a count of how often the French writer contradicted it.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots tie this to 26 across. The phrasing also echoes Peter's three denials of Christ.
explanation.definitionFit: Voltaire's quip rejects each of the three words of the empire's name, so it is denied on three occasions.

clue.text: Just part of the church, say, in the Shetlands

parts.note: just in the sense of even-handed means fair

indicators.note: say signals that the word is to be spoken rather than spelt, giving a word sounding the same

parts.note: an aisle is a passage or side section of a church

explanation.surface: Only a section of a church building, apparently, located up in Shetland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'only', but means fair. Fair Isle is a remote island in the Shetland group, famous for its patterned knitwear.
explanation.definitionFit: The island lies between Orkney and the main Shetland island and is administratively part of Shetland.
